questions.prompt: When should the inclusion criteria of a literature review be written?
options: Never; relevance is a personal judgement.
Only after the full texts are read.
Before reading abstracts, so the rule cannot drift toward papers you like.
After reading the abstracts, so you can see what is relevant.
questions.explanation: Pre-specified criteria reduce selection bias. Refinements are allowed but must be recorded.

questions.prompt: A search identifies 200 records; 40 are duplicates; 100 are excluded at title/abstract screening; 25 are excluded at full-text screening. How many papers are included?
A trusted survey lists 20 relevant papers. Your search retrieved 15 of them. What is the recall? Give a decimal.
The same search retrieved 300 records in total, 15 of which are on the survey list. What is the precision? Give a decimal.
Paper A reports 95% on dataset D1 and paper B reports 90% on dataset D2 with no prior information. What should the comparison matrix say?
options: A is better than B by 5 points, since both report the same accuracy metric on image data.
They are not directly comparable: different data, so add dataset and condition columns, not a ranking.
B is better, because it reaches 90% without any prior information while A uses a prior.
Both are equal, because both papers report accuracy above 90% on their own dataset.
questions.explanation: Results on different datasets or with different assumptions cannot be ranked without additional evidence.

questions.prompt: A comparison matrix shows no paper for 'method M under condition C'. List three possible reasons and one action to tell them apart.
rubric: Names that nobody did it, that it is infeasible or pointless, and that the search missed it.
Gives an action: differently worded searches, forward citation chasing, or a recall check against a gold list.
Concludes the gap is only a candidate until the search-failure explanation is rejected.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: You add synonyms ('laser scan', 'range finder') to the query. What is the expected effect?
options: Both always rise, because extra synonyms add only relevant papers to the results.
Precision rises and recall falls, because the added terms narrow the set of matches.
Nothing changes if the topic is the same, because the search engine already expands synonyms.
Recall tends to rise and precision tends to fall, so screening the results takes longer.
questions.explanation: More synonyms retrieve more of the relevant papers but also more irrelevant ones.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would implement an inclusion-rule function so that every excluded paper carries a reason, and why this matters.
rubric: Applies explicit checks in a fixed order (year, excluded terms, required topics) and returns the first failing reason.
Returns included papers and a list of (id, reason).
Explains that reasons make the counts auditable and let you spot a rule that is too strict.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
